The South American coati (Nasua nasua) is a medium-sized procyonid that exhibits a suite of life-history traits shaped by its tropical forest environment. At a body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], resting metabolic rate has been measured at 992 milliliters per hour of oxygen consumption [JOi = 992 milliliters per hour of oxygen consumption], a value reflecting the species' active, arboreal foraging lifestyle. Reproductive output is moderate, with a maximum of 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 pups per litter] and females typically producing one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], as recorded under thermoneutral conditions at 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. Neonates are relatively small at parturition, with a wet weight at birth of 140 grams [Wwb = 140 grams], a modest mass that belies the rapid growth required to transition to predatory independence. This altricial pattern is consistent with other procyonids of similar body size, where energy is allocated toward producing a sizable litter rather than large individual offspring.

The developmental timeline of Nasua nasua is punctuated by several critical milestones, all measured under standard physiological conditions. Within the thermal range of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], the gestation time is approximately 73 days [tg = approximately 73 days], a relatively short period compared to other carnivorans of similar mass, likely an adaptation to seasonal resource pulses in Neotropical forests. Following this, the time since birth at weaning is recorded at 86 days [tx = 86 days], at which point the young begin consuming solid food while still associating closely with the maternal group at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This extended lactation period supports the development of complex foraging behaviors, including the characteristic use of the elongated snout to probe leaf litter and soil for invertebrates and fruit. Weaning weight marks a significant energetic threshold for both mother and offspring.

At the completion of lactation, pups typically reach a wet weight at weaning of 730 grams [Wwx = 730 grams], representing a more than fivefold increase from neonatal mass and indicating a period of rapid somatic investment. The age at which female coatis attain sexual maturity is another key parameter, with the time since birth at puberty being 730 days [tp = 730 days] when measured at a body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This two-year period allows juveniles to acquire the social skills and body condition necessary for successful reproduction in a female-bonded, philopatric society. Delayed maturation in females is thought to reduce intraspecific competition for breeding opportunities within the troop, where older, more experienced females dominate access to the best foraging patches and denning sites.

Maximum lifespan is another dimension of the coati's life history that reflects its position as a medium-sized tropical carnivoran. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recorded at 23.7 years [am = 23.7 years], a remarkable longevity for an animal of this size, measured at a body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This extended lifespan likely buffers against years of low reproductive success caused by fruit shortages or environmental stochasticity, allowing females to breed over many seasons. In comparison with related species, such as the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica), the South American coati shows a slightly longer reproductive window, which may be linked to the more stable but seasonal climate of its South American range, where resource availability is less predictable than in Central America.

Adult body size in females provides a foundation for understanding their energetic and reproductive ecology. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 4750 grams [Wwi = 4750 grams], a value that places them among the smaller-bodied procyonids but still capable of defending territories and climbing efficiently. This adult mass trajectory is achieved through a prolonged period of growth following weaning, with females continuing to gain mass well beyond the age of sexual maturity. In comparative terms, the coati's adult female mass is intermediate between that of the ringtail (Bassariscus astutus) and the kinkajou (Potos flavus), reflecting diverse ecological niches within the family Procyonidae.
